hints: Look at this as two separate thermal decompositions happening side by side in the same tube.
Remember magnesium carbonate breaks down to magnesium oxide plus carbon dioxide, so gas 1 is definitely present.
Recall what a Group 2 nitrate gives on heating, an oxide plus two gases, and check if that covers the other two gases listed.
walkthrough:
**Decompose the carbonate**

Think of a carbonate as a store of CO2. On strong heating it releases that gas and leaves the metal oxide.

Chemical equation:
$$\text{MgCO}_3(s) \rightarrow \text{MgO}(s) + \text{CO}_2(g)$$

**Decompose the nitrate**

Nitrates of Group 2 metals (except the very stable ones) always decompose the same way to oxide + nitrogen dioxide + oxygen. Magnesium is high up Group 2, so it decomposes readily.

Chemical equation:
$$2\text{Mg}(\text{NO}_3)_2(s) \rightarrow 2\text{MgO}(s) + 4\text{NO}_2(g) + \text{O}_2(g)$$

**Combine the gases**

From step 1 we get carbon dioxide (1). From step 2 we get nitrogen dioxide (2) and oxygen (3). Since both solids are in the mixture, all three gases are evolved together.

options.A: Correct. Both decompositions occur. MgCO3 gives CO2 (1), and Mg(NO3)2 gives NO2 (2) plus O2 (3). So 1, 2 and 3 are all formed.
options.B: Incorrect. This combination means 1 and 2 only. It correctly includes CO2 and NO2 but wrongly leaves out oxygen, which is always formed alongside NO2 from nitrate decomposition.
options.C: Incorrect. This combination means 2 and 3 only. It correctly includes the nitrate products but wrongly leaves out carbon dioxide from the carbonate decomposition.
options.D: Incorrect. This means 1 only. It correctly includes CO2 but ignores that magnesium nitrate also decomposes on strong heating to give NO2 and O2.
